<header class="dg-head dg-head-section"><p class="dg-kicker">Chapter 6 <span class="dg-sep">•</span> <a href="index.html">Covariant Derivative</a></p><h1 class="dg-title"><span class="dg-secnum">6.2</span> Connection Coefficient Functions</h1></header>
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-1">
<li><p>Let <span class="math inline">\((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\)</span> be a chart. Since a connection is local<sup class="dg-fnref"><a href="#fn-4" id="fnref-4" role="doc-noteref" aria-label="Footnote 4">4</a></sup>, it also acts on tensor fields defined only over <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{U}\)</span>, such as <span class="math inline">\(\partial x_j\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(dx^j\)</span>. To determine the freedom left by the axioms, consider <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X}_p = x^i_p \, (\partial x_i)_p\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\left. \mathcal{Y} \right|_\mathcal{U} = \tilde{x}^j \, \partial x_j\)</span>. Property 4 and the product rule give  <span class="math display">\[
            \nabla_{\mathcal{X}_p} \mathcal{Y}
            = x^i_p \, \nabla_{(\partial x_i)_p} \big( \tilde{x}^j \, \partial x_j \big)
            = \mathcal{X}_p(\tilde{x}^j) \, (\partial x_j)_p
            + x^i_p \, \tilde{x}^j(p) \, \nabla_{(\partial x_i)_p} \partial x_j .
        \]</span>  The first term is fixed by the axioms. The only data left free are the vectors <span class="math inline">\(\nabla_{(\partial x_i)_p} \partial x_j \in T_p\mathcal{M}\)</span>, whose components define the <strong>connection coefficient functions</strong> of <span class="math inline">\(\nabla\)</span> w.r.t. the chart <span class="math inline">\((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\)</span>:  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}\right)^i_{jk} : \mathcal{U} &amp;\longrightarrow \mathbb{R} \\
            p &amp;\longmapsto \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}\right)^i_{jk}(p) \coloneqq
            (dx^i)_p\big( \nabla_{(\partial x_k)_p} \partial x_j \big),
        \end{align*}</span>  i.e. <span class="math inline">\(\nabla_{(\partial x_k)_p} \partial x_j = \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}\right)^i_{jk}(p) \, (\partial x_i)_p\)</span>, or, at field level, <span class="math inline">\(\nabla_{\partial x_k} \partial x_j = \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}\right)^i_{jk} \, \partial x_i\)</span>. Note the index convention: the <em>last</em> lower index labels the direction of differentiation. The components of <span class="math inline">\(\nabla_{\mathcal{X}_p} \mathcal{Y}\)</span> therefore read  <span class="math display">\[
            \left( \nabla_{\mathcal{X}_p} \mathcal{Y} \right)^k \coloneqq (dx^k)_p\big( \nabla_{\mathcal{X}_p} \mathcal{Y} \big)
            = \mathcal{X}_p(\tilde{x}^k) + \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}\right)^k_{ji}(p) \, \tilde{x}^j(p) \, x^i_p ,
        \]</span>  or, letting the direction vary with a vector field <span class="math inline">\(\left. \mathcal{X} \right|_\mathcal{U} = x^i \, \partial x_i\)</span>, <span class="math inline">\(\left( \nabla_\mathcal{X} \mathcal{Y} \right)^k = \mathcal{X}\left\lfloor \tilde{x}^k \right\rceil + \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}\right)^k_{ji} \, \tilde{x}^j \, x^i\)</span>. The <span class="math inline">\(\dim(\mathcal{M})^3\)</span> functions <span class="math inline">\(\left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}\right)^i_{jk}\)</span> thus fully determine the action of <span class="math inline">\(\nabla\)</span> on vector fields over <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{U}\)</span>.</p></li>
<li><p>Analogously, for a covector field <span class="math inline">\(\left. \mathsf{X} \right|_\mathcal{U} = \mathtt{x}_j \, dx^j\)</span>,  <span class="math display">\[
            \nabla_{\mathcal{X}_p} \mathsf{X}
            = x^i_p \, \nabla_{(\partial x_i)_p} \big( \mathtt{x}_j \, dx^j \big)
            = \mathcal{X}_p(\mathtt{x}_j) \, (dx^j)_p
            + x^i_p \, \mathtt{x}_j(p) \, \nabla_{(\partial x_i)_p} dx^j ,
        \]</span>  where the data left free are now the covectors <span class="math inline">\(\nabla_{(\partial x_i)_p} dx^j \in T_p^*\mathcal{M}\)</span>, with components  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            \big(\tilde{\Gamma}_\mathscr{X}\big)^i_{jk} : \mathcal{U} &amp;\longrightarrow \mathbb{R} \\
            p &amp;\longmapsto \big(\tilde{\Gamma}_\mathscr{X}\big)^i_{jk}(p) \coloneqq
            \big( \nabla_{(\partial x_k)_p} dx^i \big)\big( (\partial x_j)_p \big),
        \end{align*}</span>  i.e. <span class="math inline">\(\nabla_{\partial x_k} dx^i = \big(\tilde{\Gamma}_\mathscr{X}\big)^i_{jk} \, dx^j\)</span>. These, however, are not independent of the <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}\)</span>’s. Applying the Leibniz rule to the constant functions <span class="math inline">\(dx^j\left\lceil \partial x_k \right\rfloor = \delta^j_k\)</span>, whose covariant derivative vanishes by property 1,  <span class="math display">\[
            0 = \nabla_{(\partial x_i)_p}\big( dx^j \left\lceil \partial x_k \right\rfloor  \big) = \big( \nabla_{(\partial x_i)_p} dx^j \big)\big( (\partial x_k)_p \big)
            + (dx^j)_p\big( \nabla_{(\partial x_i)_p} \partial x_k \big)
            = \big(\tilde{\Gamma}_\mathscr{X}\big)^j_{ki}(p) + \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}\right)^j_{ki}(p),
        \]</span>  so that <span class="math inline">\(\tilde{\Gamma}_\mathscr{X} = -\Gamma_\mathscr{X}\)</span>, and the components of <span class="math inline">\(\nabla_{\mathcal{X}_p} \mathsf{X}\)</span> read  <span class="math display">\[
            \left( \nabla_{\mathcal{X}_p} \mathsf{X} \right)_k \coloneqq \left( \nabla_{\mathcal{X}_p} \mathsf{X} \right)\big( (\partial x_k)_p \big)
            = \mathcal{X}_p(\mathtt{x}_k) - \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}\right)^j_{ki}(p) \, \mathtt{x}_j(p) \, x^i_p .
        \]</span>  Repeated use of the Leibniz rule gives the action of <span class="math inline">\(\nabla\)</span> on tensor fields of any valence: every upper index contributes a <span class="math inline">\(+\Gamma_\mathscr{X}\)</span> term, and every lower index a <span class="math inline">\(-\Gamma_\mathscr{X}\)</span> term. For instance, for a <span class="math inline">\((1,1)\)</span>-tensor field with components <span class="math inline">\(T^i_j\)</span>,  <span class="math display">\[
            \left( \nabla_\mathcal{X} T \right)^i_{j}
            = \mathcal{X}\left\lfloor T^i_{j} \right\rceil
            + \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}\right)^i_{m\ell} \, T^m_{j} \, x^\ell
            - \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}\right)^m_{j\ell} \, T^i_{m} \, x^\ell.
        \]</span></p></li>
<li><p>Let us now derive how the connection coefficient functions transform under a change of chart. On <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V}\)</span>, with the transformation laws of Section <a class="dg-xref" href="../fields/tensor-fields-and-notation.html" data-kind="section" data-label="section_Tensor_Fields_and_notation">5.3</a>, <span class="math inline">\(dy^i = \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i}{\partial \mathscr{X}^l} \, dx^l\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\partial y_j = \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^s}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} \, \partial x_s\)</span>, the <span class="math inline">\(C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\)</span>-linearity in the direction and the product rule give  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{Y}\right)^i_{jk}
            &amp;\coloneqq dy^i\left\lceil \nabla_{\partial y_k} \partial y_j \right\rfloor
            = \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i}{\partial \mathscr{X}^l} \, \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^p}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k} \,
            dx^l\left\lceil \nabla_{\partial x_p} \left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^s}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} \, \partial x_s \right) \right\rfloor \\
            &amp;= \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i}{\partial \mathscr{X}^l} \, \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^p}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k} \,
            dx^l\left\lceil \partial x_p\left\lfloor \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^s}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} \right\rceil \partial x_s
            + \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^s}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} \, \nabla_{\partial x_p} \partial x_s \right\rfloor \\
            &amp;= \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i}{\partial \mathscr{X}^s} \,
            \underbrace{\frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^p}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k} \, \partial x_p}_{\partial y_k}
            \left\lfloor \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^s}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} \right\rceil
            + \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i}{\partial \mathscr{X}^l} \, \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^p}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k} \,
            \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^s}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} \,
            \underbrace{dx^l\left\lceil \nabla_{\partial x_p} \partial x_s \right\rfloor}_{\left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}\right)^l_{sp}},
        \end{align*}</span>  where we used <span class="math inline">\(dx^l\left\lceil \partial x_s \right\rfloor = \delta^l_s\)</span>. The first term contains the basis field <span class="math inline">\(\partial y_k\)</span> acting on the smooth function <span class="math inline">\(\frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^s}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} : p \mapsto \partial_j \left[ \mathscr{X}^s \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} \right] \big( \mathscr{Y}(p) \big)\)</span>. Since <span class="math inline">\(\frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^s}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} = \partial_j \left[ \mathscr{X}^s \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} \right]\)</span>, the definition of the chart-induced basis gives  <span class="math display">\[
            \frac{\partial^2 \mathscr{X}^s}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k \, \partial \mathscr{Y}^j}(p) \coloneqq
            \partial y_k\left\lfloor \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^s}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} \right\rceil (p)
            = \partial_k \partial_j \left[ \mathscr{X}^s \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} \right] \big( \mathscr{Y}(p) \big),
        \]</span>  an ordinary second partial derivative of the chart transition map <span class="math inline">\(\textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}}\)</span>, which is smooth since the atlas is <span class="math inline">\(C^\infty\)</span>-compatible, and symmetric in <span class="math inline">\(j\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(k\)</span> by Schwarz’s theorem. We thus arrive at the transformation law  <span class="math display">\[
            \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{Y}\right)^i_{jk}
            = \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i}{\partial \mathscr{X}^s} \, \frac{\partial^2 \mathscr{X}^s}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k \, \partial \mathscr{Y}^j}
            + \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i}{\partial \mathscr{X}^l} \, \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^s}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} \,
            \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^p}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k} \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}\right)^l_{sp}.
        \]</span>  The second term is exactly the transformation law of the components of a <span class="math inline">\((1,2)\)</span>-tensor field. The first one, involving second derivatives of the chart transition map, shows that the connection coefficient functions are <em>not</em> the components of a tensor field.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Normal coordinates.</strong> The inhomogeneous term can be exploited to simplify the connection coefficient functions at a chosen point. Let <span class="math inline">\(p \in \mathcal{U}\)</span> and assume, w.l.o.g. (translating the chart), <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{X}(p) = (0, \dots, 0)\)</span>. Define a new chart <span class="math inline">\((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})\)</span> around <span class="math inline">\(p\)</span> through the transition map  <span class="math display">\[
            \left( \mathscr{Y}^i \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \right)(\alpha^1, \dots, \alpha^d) \coloneqq
            \alpha^i + \frac{1}{2} \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}\right)^i_{(jk)}(p) \, \alpha^j \alpha^k,
            \qquad
            \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}\right)^i_{(jk)} \coloneqq \frac{1}{2} \Big[ \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}\right)^i_{jk} + \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}\right)^i_{kj} \Big],
        \]</span>  which, by the inverse function theorem (the Jacobian of this transition map at <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{X}(p) = 0\)</span> is the identity), defines a chart on some neighbourhood <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{U}\)</span> of <span class="math inline">\(p\)</span>, <span class="math inline">\(C^\infty\)</span>-compatible with every chart of <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{A}\)</span>. It therefore belongs to the maximal atlas determined by <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{A}\)</span> (see the footnote to the definition of a smooth manifold in Chapter <a class="dg-xref" href="../topological-manifolds/index.html" data-kind="chapter" data-label="chapter_Topological_Manifolds">3</a>), which is the atlas we always tacitly work with<sup class="dg-fnref"><a href="#fn-5" id="fnref-5" role="doc-noteref" aria-label="Footnote 5">5</a></sup>. Its first and second derivatives at <span class="math inline">\(p\)</span> are  <span class="math display">\[
            \left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i}{\partial \mathscr{X}^j} \right)_p = \delta^i_j = \left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^i}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} \right)_p,
            \qquad
            \left( \frac{\partial^2 \mathscr{Y}^i}{\partial \mathscr{X}^k \, \partial \mathscr{X}^j} \right)_p = \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}\right)^i_{(jk)}(p).
        \]</span>  Writing the transformation law with the roles of the two charts exchanged, and evaluating it at <span class="math inline">\(p\)</span>,  <span class="math display">\[
            \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}\right)^i_{jk}(p) = \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}\right)^i_{(jk)}(p) + \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{Y}\right)^i_{jk}(p)
            \, \longrightarrow \,
            \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{Y}\right)^i_{jk}(p) = \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}\right)^i_{[jk]}(p) \coloneqq
            \frac{1}{2} \Big[ \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}\right)^i_{jk}(p) - \left(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}\right)^i_{kj}(p) \Big].
        \]</span>  The symmetric part of the connection coefficient functions can thus always be made to vanish at any chosen point, whereas the antisymmetric part cannot: it is, up to a factor <span class="math inline">\(-1/2\)</span>, the torsion introduced below, a tensor field, which vanishes in one chart if and only if it vanishes in all of them. Note also that this holds at the single point <span class="math inline">\(p\)</span> only: the derivatives of the <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma\)</span>’s cannot, in general, be removed, which is related to the curvature introduced below.</p></li>
</ul>
<section class="dg-footnotes" role="doc-endnotes"><div class="dg-fn" id="fn-4" role="doc-footnote"><a class="dg-fn-num" href="#fnref-4" aria-label="Back to the text">4</a><div class="dg-fn-body"><p>If <span class="math inline">\(T\)</span> vanishes on an open neighbourhood <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{W}\)</span> of <span class="math inline">\(p\)</span>, then <span class="math inline">\(\nabla_{\mathcal{X}_p} T = 0\)</span>. Indeed, take <span class="math inline">\(\psi \in C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\)</span> with <span class="math inline">\(\psi(p) = 0\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\psi = 1\)</span> outside a compact subset of <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{W}\)</span> (one minus a bump function around <span class="math inline">\(p\)</span>). Then <span class="math inline">\(T = \psi \, T\)</span>, and the product rule gives <span class="math inline">\(\nabla_{\mathcal{X}_p} T = \mathcal{X}_p(\psi) \, T_p + \psi(p) \, \nabla_{\mathcal{X}_p} T = 0\)</span>, since <span class="math inline">\(T_p = 0\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\psi(p) = 0\)</span>. Hence <span class="math inline">\(\nabla_{\mathcal{X}_p} T\)</span> only depends on <span class="math inline">\(T\)</span> near <span class="math inline">\(p\)</span>.</p></div></div><div class="dg-fn" id="fn-5" role="doc-footnote"><a class="dg-fn-num" href="#fnref-5" aria-label="Back to the text">5</a><div class="dg-fn-body"><p>In much of the literature, “normal coordinates” refers to the coordinates built from the autoparallels through <span class="math inline">\(p\)</span> (the exponential map). The quadratic construction used here is the minimal one achieving <span class="math inline">\(\left(\Gamma_\mathscr{Y}\right)^i_{(jk)}(p) = 0\)</span>, which is all we need.</p></div></div></section>
